questions.text: Why can Monte Carlo value estimates have high variance on long episodes compared with one-step TD estimates?

options.A: Monte Carlo uses exact transition probabilities for every future state.
options.B: Monte Carlo uses the full sampled future return, including distant random outcomes.
options.C: Monte Carlo averages only immediate rewards and ignores later outcomes.
options.D: Monte Carlo updates from a bootstrapped next-state value each step.

questions.explanation: Monte Carlo waits for the entire observed return, so distant random outcomes affect the estimate; one-step TD bootstraps from a next-state estimate instead.

questions.text: A policy is evaluated from complete episodes, but one state was visited in only 8 of them. The lesson’s shipped evaluator requires at least 100 episodes per state before reporting a tabular estimate. What should the evaluator do?

options.A: Report the estimate as reliable because 8 complete returns have no sampling variance.
options.B: Increase sampling until that state has enough visits, or withhold its estimate.
options.C: Fill in the missing visits with zero returns and report a 100-sample mean.
options.D: Replace the state estimate with the maximum return seen elsewhere.

questions.explanation: With only 8 episode visits, the stated reporting threshold is unmet. Collect more coverage or do not report that state estimate as ready.

questions.text: A rollout records (s,a,r) before checking done. If env.step returns done=True on the second move, how many transition tuples are in the returned trajectory?

options.A: One, because the terminal move is excluded.
options.B: Two, because the terminal move is appended before breaking.
options.C: Three, because the loop adds an extra terminal transition.
options.D: Zero, because the trajectory is cleared when done is true.

questions.explanation: The code appends the current transition before the done check. It records both moves, then breaks after the second one.
